respectively. The equation for uu in the outer region then becomes

Du​d​u2d​x2+c​δ−δ​u−∑i=1nρu​L​δ​(x−xi)=0\displaystyle D_{u}\frac{d{}^{2}u}{dx^{2}}+c\delta-\delta u-\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{\rho}{u}L\delta(x-x_{i})=0 (13)

with ρ=6​DvL​δ​γ+δβ\rho=6\frac{\sqrt{D_{v}}}{L}\frac{\delta\sqrt{\gamma+\delta}}{\beta} and where we have used that, according to the spike approximation, β​u​(u+vo​u​t)2−(γ+δ)​vo​u​t≈0\beta u(u+v_{out})^{2}-(\gamma+\delta)v_{out}\approx 0 (from equation Eq. (2b)) to simplify the contribution away from the spike. Note the inverse dependence on uu in the point sink term (which we call an inverted sink). This form is also obtained for other Turing systems with a u​v2uv^{2} non-linearity, such as the Schnakenberg and Brusselator models [47, 31].

Following the approach of the previous section, the solution to equation Eq. (13) is given by

u⁡(x)=c−∑iρi′​G​(x,xi),u(x)=c-\sum_{i}\rho^{\prime}_{i}G(x;x_{i})~, (14)

where the Green’s function is defined as for point sinks but in terms of the corresponding dimensionless parameter κ=L​δDu\kappa=L\sqrt{\frac{\delta}{D_{u}}}, the ratio of the length of the domain to the diffusive length scale of uu (henceforth κ\kappa replaces bb in the set of dimensionless parameters of the system). The coefficients ρi′=ρi′​(𝒙)\rho^{\prime}_{i}=\rho^{\prime}_{i}(\bm{x}) are now determined by the non-linear algebraic system

ρi′=σ​c2u⁡(xi)i=1,…,n.\rho^{\prime}_{i}=\sigma\frac{c^{2}}{u(x_{i})}\quad i=1,\ldots,n~. (15)

where σ=ρc2​δ=6​b+1a​Γ\sigma=\frac{\rho}{c^{2}\delta}=6\frac{\sqrt{b+1}}{a\sqrt{\Gamma}} is the second dimensionless parameter of Eq. (13). The inverse dependence on u⁡(xi)u(x_{i}) makes solving this algebraic system challenging. For a general choice of sink positions xix_{i}, there are nn coupled quadratic equations in ρi′\rho^{\prime}_{i}, and therefore up to 2n2^{n} real solutions. However, this multiplicity of solutions collapses in the spike limit σ→0\sigma\rightarrow 0, in which the only physical solution is 22 2 In the limit σ→0\sigma\rightarrow 0, equation Eq. (15) becomes ρi′​(c−∑jρj′​G​(xi,xj))=0\rho^{\prime}_{i}(c-\sum_{j}\rho^{\prime}_{j}G(x_{i};x_{j}))=0. Since taking any ρi′=0\rho^{\prime}_{i}=0 gives a solution of the system without the iith spike, these are unphysical solutions.

𝝆′=c​𝑮−1​𝒆^\bm{\rho}^{\prime}=c~\bm{G}^{-1}\hat{\bm{e}} (16)

where 𝑮i​j=G⁡(xi,xj)\bm{G}_{ij}=G(x_{i};x_{j}) and 𝒆^\hat{\bm{e}} is the column vector with all unit entries. This is precisely the same solution obtained in the perfect sink limit λ→∞\lambda\rightarrow\infty of the point sink system (Eq. (4) and Eq. (6)). Thus, in the singular spike limit, steady-state solutions of the Turing system are equivalent to that of a system of perfect sinks, a surprising equivalence given the inverted pre-factor in Eq. (13).

We next solve the system for a single arbitrarily positioned spike. We find two solutions corresponding to different spike amplitudes

ρ1,±′c=1±1−4​σ​G​(x1,x1)2​G​(x1,x1).\frac{\rho^{\prime}_{1,\pm}}{c}=\frac{1\pm\sqrt{1-4\sigma G(x_{1};x_{1})}}{2G(x_{1};x_{1})}~.

and corresponding masses M1,±=c−ρ±′M_{1,\pm}=c-\rho^{\prime}_{\pm}. Since we only ever observe spikes within large amplitudes, i.e. patterns in which almost all the mass of the system is contained with spikes, we assume that the low amplitude solution is unphysical for finite σ\sigma and not only in the spike limit σ→0\sigma\rightarrow 0 (or unstable in the context of the time-dependent system, see below). Defining the flux-differential across a spike analogously to equation Eq. (7),

ΔJi(𝒙)=−Du2∑jρj′[Gx(xi+;xj)+Gx(xi−;xj)],\Delta J_{i}(\bm{x})=-\frac{D_{u}}{2}\sum_{j}\rho^{\prime}_{j}\left[G_{x}(x_{i}^{+};x_{j})+G_{x}(x_{i}^{-};x_{j})\right], (17)

we find a linear dependence on the spike position in the regime κ≪1\kappa\ll 1

Δ​J1c​δ​L\displaystyle\frac{\Delta J_{1}}{c\delta L} =−12​ρ+′c​sinh⁡(2​κ​x1L)sinh⁡(κ)\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{2}\frac{\rho^{\prime}_{+}}{c}\frac{\sinh(2\kappa\frac{x_{1}}{L})}{\sinh(\kappa)} (18)
≈−(1+1−4​σ)2​x1L+𝒪⁡(κ2),\displaystyle\approx-\frac{\left(1+\sqrt{1-4\sigma}\right)}{2}\frac{x_{1}}{L}+\mathcal{O}(\kappa^{2})~,

consistent with our numerical observations (Fig. 4A,B) and just as we found for the non-inverted sinks in the previous section (Fig. 3C). Furthermore in the spike limit, σ→0\sigma\rightarrow 0, Δ​J1=c​δ​x1\Delta J_{1}=c\delta x_{1} is linear in δ\delta, consistent with our numerical observations (for which σ=0.0463\sigma=0.0463) (Fig. 2B). We also find that M1+M_{1+}, the total mass of uu, is minimised at mid-domain (Fig. 4B). However, while the mass and flux differential displayed very similar qualitative profiles (Fig. 4B), the agreement was not quantitative. This is likely due to the nature of the approximation and/or because our solution is not sufficiently spike-like. We will see in the next section that our main result is unaffected.

The observations that peaks in a Turing pattern move with a velocity proportional to the flux-differential across them (Fig. 2A,B, Fig. 4A, Fig. S3) suggests that the spike approximation can be extended to account for spike movement by specifying the spike velocities as

d​xid​t=ν​Δ​Ji​(𝒙),\frac{dx_{i}}{dt}=\nu\Delta J_{i}(\bm{x})~, (19)

where ν\nu is some unknown parameter. By the correspondence with point sinks, this expression becomes equivalent in the spike σ→0\sigma\rightarrow 0 and long diffusive length-scale κ→0\kappa\rightarrow 0 to a description in which the mass MM acts as potential and the sinks as over-damped particles as in Eq. (11). Together with Eq. (15), Eq. (19) defines a differential-algebraic system for the dynamics of nn spikes. However, not all spike configurations are stable. Based on our numerical observations, stable solutions consist only of regularly positioned spikes of the same height (ρi′=ρ′\rho^{\prime}_{i}=\rho^{\prime}), also referred to as symmetric spike solutions, just as for the Turing system itself. Consistent with this, the flux-differentials of these solutions vanish, Δ​Ji​(𝒙¯)=0\Delta J_{i}(\bar{\bm{x}})=0, via the properties of the Green’s function, just as for the points sinks of the previous section (and Appendix A).

As an example, we consider the case of two spikes. For our parameter set the system then has up to four real solutions for each configuration (x1,x2)(x_{1},x_{2}). In Fig. 4D, we show sample trajectories (of the real solution branch with the smallest mass MM; the other real solutions leads to very weak sinks and almost uniform u⁡(x)u(x)). The similarity to the numerical observation (Fig. 4C) and the system of point sinks in the previous section (Fig. 3D) is apparent. In both cases, the steady-state solution consists of quarter position peaks/spikes and minimises the mass of uu.

Let us summarise our results. We have shown that the movement and positioning of peaks in a Turing pattern is akin to that of a system of moving point sinks. Firstly, the regular, periodic steady-state positions are a result of the flow (creation, diffusion, decay) of mass through the system, and not by some dominant linear mode. The steady-state configuration is the one for which all the flux-differentials balance and this is also the configuration that minimises the total mass of the fast species. We found empirically that the movement of peaks (in the slow species) is well described by the peak velocity being proportional to the flux-differential of the fast species across it. Furthermore, in the spike limit, this is equivalent to the total mass of the fast species acting as a potential through which the peaks move as over-damped particles. While this does not imply that the mass or some other function acts as a potential away from this limit (i.e. that Δ​𝑱\Delta\bm{J} is a conservative vector field in general), the mass is nonetheless minimal at the steady-state configurations (Fig. 4A,C). In the next section, we will see that we can use the stead-state mass to compare the ‘energy’ of patterns with different numbers of peaks and in this way predict the preferred number of peaks at steady state, and not just their positions.

Competition and Pattern Selection

We have seen that in the mass-conserved limit δ→0\delta\rightarrow 0, the model exhibits a complete coarsening effect in which the only stable patterns consist of a singe peak positioned somewhere in the interior of the domain (Fig. 2D) or, on a short domain, an interface. We have also seen that for small δ\delta the model exhibits incomplete coarsening. With our default parameters (with L=4L=4), linear stability predicts that mode n=8n=8 (four peaks) will dominate (Fig. 1A). While this is true initially, the pattern subsequently coarsens so that we most frequently obtain two peaks (dominated by mode n=4n=4)(Fig. 1B,C, S1D). This coarsening effect is also referred to as a competition instability and has previously been studied in the context of spike solutions [32, 33, 31]. To our knowledge, there is currently no way to determine which pattern is finally obtained. Note that this is a narrower question than asking which patterns are stable, since Turing systems are in general multi-stable.

This motivated us to explore the connection between coarsening and the flow rate δ\delta in more detail. We measured the distribution of steady state patterns obtained for different values of δ\delta (through the dimensionless parameter κ\kappa) and compared against the prediction of linear instability (Fig 5A,B). We used periodic boundary conditions to avoid peaks on the boundary that are not described by the spike approximation. We found that for κ≳1\kappa\gtrsim 1 linearly stability analysis correctly predicts the dominant mode at steady state. However, for κ≲1\kappa\lesssim 1, a coarsening process occurs and the steady-state pattern is dominated by a lower mode than that predicted. Given our previous observations on the role of the diffusive length-scale, we explain these results as follows. When the diffusive length-scale is longer than the domain size, all peaks compete for uu molecules created across the domain. Whereas, when the length-scale is short, peaks only absorb molecules of uu created within a distance given by the diffusive length-scale and therefore compete less or not at all. Competition is also exasperated by the fact that decreasing δ\delta also decreases the total flux through the system (c​δ​Lc\delta L).

We next applied the spike approximation developed in the previous section. We decreased DvD_{v} from the default value so that the obtained pattern was reasonably spike-like (Fig. 5C) while at the same time not resulting in a very much enlarged Turing space (since we want to sweep over different values of δ\delta). We considered only symmetric, regularly positioned spike solutions, which are the only observed steady-state solutions. For nn spikes, we obtain two possible values of ρ′\rho^{\prime}, of which we take the larger, ρ+′\rho^{\prime}_{+} (the other corresponds to extremely weak spikes i.e. ρ−′≈0\rho^{\prime}_{-}\approx 0). This gives a solution u⁡(x)=c−ρ+′​∑iG⁡(x,x¯i)u(x)=c-\rho^{\prime}_{+}\sum_{i}G(x;\bar{x}_{i}) with mass

M/c=1−n​1+1−2​κ​σ​coth⁡(κ2​n)κ​coth⁡(κ2​n).M/c=1-n\frac{1+\sqrt{1-2\kappa\sigma\coth(\frac{\kappa}{2n})}}{\kappa\coth(\frac{\kappa}{2n})}~. (20)

Note that for a real solution we must have 1>2​κ​σ​coth⁡(κ2​n)1>2\kappa\sigma\coth(\frac{\kappa}{2n}). Therefore, for a given choice of parameters, there is an upper bound on the number of spikes that a solution can contain. In general, a solution exists for multiple values of nn. However, numerically, we observe a very narrow distribution of the number of peaks (Fig. S1, Fig. 5F). We hypothesised that mass minimisation might play a role. Indeed, when we examined the mass MM of solutions consisting of different numbers of spikes at there respective steady-state positions, we found that the mass is minimal for a specific number of spikes (Fig. 5D). This could also be seen by plotting the mass as a function of κ\kappa for different values of nn (Fig. S4). The value of nn at the minimum decreases with κ\kappa, with a single spike being minimal at κ→0\kappa\rightarrow 0. The curves invert so that as κ\kappa is increased multiple spikes produce the lowest mass. Given that we have already shown that the mass of u⁡(x)u(x) is minimal at the steady-state, we hypothesised that it could also be used to compare solutions with different numbers of peaks and therefore identify a preferred ‘minimum energy’ state.

We compared the number of spikes predicted by this mass minimisation principle against the distribution of patterns obtained numerically (starting from a small random perturbation around the uniform state). We found remarkable agreement (Fig. 5E, red circles). Mass minimisation correctly predicts the most frequent pattern obtained over the entire range of κ\kappa, including, most importantly, the regime in which coarsening occurs. There is significant deviation only at the transition points and close to exiting the Turing regime at high κ\kappa. In comparison, the linear prediction only agrees for the highest values of κ\kappa i.e. close to onset (Fig. 5E, green triangles). Remarkably, the prediction was also reasonably accurate even when the solution is not very spike like, as for our default parameter set (Fig. S5) and towards the boundary of the Turing space (Fig. 2). Thus, mass minimisation not only explains where the peaks of a Turing pattern are positioned but also how many peaks there will be at steady-state, after any coarsening has taken place. Importantly, it does so far from onset and hence outside the region where weakly non-linear approaches such as the amplitude equations are valid.

To investigate the general applicability of these results, we performed a similar analysis of the Brusselator model (Appendix C). This model also exhibits coarsening when the flow of mass through the system is slow (Fig. 6A,B). Using a similar analytic approximation as before, we obtained an expression for symmetric n-spike solutions (Appendix C). We found that the total mass of the fast species

M=OPEN6​n​(b+1)3/2)a​Γ+Γ​b12​n2​b​(n+1),M=\frac{6n(b+1)^{3/2})}{a\sqrt{\Gamma}}+\frac{\Gamma b}{12n^{2}b(n+1)}, (21)

is again minimised for a particular number n=ncn=n_{c} of spikes and we found this minimum to be an excellent predictor of the final pattern obtained after coarsening (Fig. 6C). Thus mass minimisation may serve as a general principle for coarsening and pattern selection in Turing systems.

Discussion

One of the main challenges for the physics of pattern formation is the prediction of which pattern will be obtained, not only at onset, i.e. at entry into the parameter space giving patterns, but generically for any parameter values. While linear stability analysis can give a prediction for the dominant mode, non-linear effects mean that it can be inaccurate. Furthermore, as we have argued, linear analysis cannot explain the periodic nature of final patterns nor (with reflexive boundary conditions) the positioning of peaks within the domain, which occurs dynamically in several settings that are outside of the linear regime (e.g. domain growth, coarsening, initialised peaks). Weakly non-linear approaches, such as the use of the method of amplitude equations, do exist but they are much less useful far from onset and while a recent phase-space approach has been introduced to study steady-state patterns in two-component mass-conserved systems [49, 50], we still lack a general theory of pattern dynamics and selection far from onset.

Here, we have presented a generalisable physical principle that can explain the positioning and preferred steady-state number of peaks in a Turing system Eq. (2). To our knowledge, mass minimization is the first framework that can predict the final steady-state pattern in the presence of coarsening i.e. which of the generally several stable patterns is preferentially selected. Our expectation is that this will guide the development of new non-linear approaches for the study of pattern selection, far from onset. The insight came from analysing the behaviour of a diffusive system consisting of point sinks that move with a velocity proportional to the gradient. We showed that the flow of mass through such a system leads to sinks being positioned symmetrically and evenly spaced across the domain (regularly positioned), as this is the unique configuration for which the gradient across each sink vanishes. Importantly, we showed that this configuration also uniquely minimises the total mass in the system. Consistent with this we showed that in the long diffusive length-scale and perfect sink limit, the total mass acts as a potential and the sinks as over-damped particles.

We found that in the Turing system, peaks (of the slowly diffusing species vv) also move toward the regularly positioned configuration, with the same dynamics as point sinks and, in doing so, minimise the total mass of the fast species uu. In the singular limit Dv≪DuD_{v}\ll D_{u}, in which the peaks of the Turing pattern become narrow point-like spikes, an analytical approximation showed that uu is indeed described by diffusion in the presence of point sinks but where the Dirac delta function terms have a 1/u1/u pre-factor. This ‘inverted’ sink term leads to the total mass of uu having a non-trivial dependence on the number of spikes and the rate of mass flow through the system. As a result, there is a critical number of spikes (and hence wavelength) that minimises the mass of uu. We therefore hypothesised that the mass could act as a multi-well potential, i.e. that it could be used to assign, at least at the steady-state, an energy to patterns with different numbers of peaks and thereby identify the preferred steady-state. In particular, we asked whether it could predict the steady-state pattern obtained after the coarsening that occurs in our model. We found that this ‘mass minimisation’ principle could indeed predict, almost perfectly, agreement the obtained patterns (Fig. 5E) and we confirmed this for another Turing system that exhibits coarsening (i.e. disagreement with the linear prediction), the Brusselator (Fig. 6). In conclusion, the peaks of a Turing pattern move according to the flux-differential of the substrate species across them and both the number and positions of peaks at steady state are such that the mass of the substrate species is minimised.

The predicted number of peaks decreases with the flow of mass through the system, with the minimal mass occurring for a single peak in the mass-conserved limit. Therefore mass minimisation also provides a physical explanation for the complete coarsening down to a single peak observed in two-component mass-conserved systems [34, 35]. Our previous three-component mass-conserved model [12], consisting of a two-component Turing system coupled linearly to a third species, did not display such complete coarsening. The role of mass flow provides the explanation. In the three-component mass-conserved system, there is still mass flow through the Turing subsystem and the rate of flow controls the strength of the competition, similar to the current model. Thus mass-minimisation appears to be a fundamental principle behind the behaviour of Turing systems and likely pattern forming systems in general.

Are our results applicable to other systems? If mass minimisation of the fast (substrate) species is central to Turing patterning, then the mass should be minimisable. In our model, the total mass of the system ∫u+v​𝑑x\int u+v~dx at steady state is fixed. In the Gray-Scott model [51] a different positive linear combination of the two species is fixed, while in the Schnackenberg and Brusselator models it is the total mass of the slow species. What happens then in models that have the mass of the fast species fixed? We consider the following class of systems:

∂tu\displaystyle\partial_{t}u =Du​∂x2u−f⁡(u,v)+a−u\displaystyle=D_{u}\partial^{2}_{x}u-f(u,v)+a-u
∂tv\displaystyle\partial_{t}v =Dv​∂x2v+f⁡(u,v)+b\displaystyle=D_{v}\partial^{2}_{x}v+f(u,v)+b

with Dv<DuD_{v}<D_{u}. Note that at steady state the mass of uu is fixed. It is straightforward to show (see Supporting Information) that a system of this form cannot admit a Turing instability for any ff, consistent with a general principle of mass minimisation. This result holds even if we replace uu in the last term by any function g⁡(u)g(u) with g′​(u)>0g^{\prime}(u)>0 at the homogeneous fixed point, and a correspondingly different measure for the mass of uu. Thus, at least for the class of models above, the total mass of the fast species at steady state must not not generically be a fixed constant. Equivalently stated, systems in which mass leaves the system through only the fast species cannot exhibit a Turing instability.

The outer equation for uu obtained in the singular limit Dv≪DuD_{v}\ll D_{u} (Eq. (13)), has the same form in other systems of the substrate-depletion type such as the Schnakenberg [47] and Brusselator [31] and indeed both of these model exhibit the same peak movement towards regular positioning (see Supporting Information). Substrate-inhibition models that have peaks of the two species overlapping, such as that of Gierer and Meinhardt [52], also exhibit peak movement towards regular positions. However, the outer equation of these models have a point source term rather than a point sink [53]. The effect of this on mass minimisation remains to be tested.

Our results indicate that both the final position and number of peaks of a Turing pattern are such that the mass of the fast species is minimal. There is therefore minimisation with respect to nn continuous variables (the peak positions) and with respect to the discrete variable nn itself. Might the mass or some other function act as potential for the dynamics of peaks? Could it determine which peaks coarsen and when? This remains to be seen but the answer may be connected to the changes in the existence and/or stability of the different solution branches of the differential-algebraic system Eq. (19). Finally, unlike flux-balance, mass minimisation extends naturally beyond point sinks and to higher dimensions. It may therefore be useful in the study of more complicated structures such as the stripes, hexagons and spots that appear in two dimensions, especially far from onset.

Numerical Methods

The simulations were performed in a spatial lattice x∈[−L2,L2]x\in[-\frac{L}{2},\frac{L}{2}] and time domain t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T], where LL is the length of the spatial domain and TT, the total time. The MATLAB solver p​d​e​p​epdepe was used to solve the time-dependent equation Eq. (2). The simulations were performed with the following default parameters (unless explicitly stated otherwise):

Du=0.3,Dv=0.012,L=2,c=300,β=1.5×10−4,γ=3.6,δ=0.014.\displaystyle\begin{split}D_{u}=0.3,D_{v}=0.012,L=2,c=300,\\ \beta=1.5\times 10^{-}4,\gamma=3.6,\delta=0.014.\end{split} (22)

the equivalent dimensionless parameters are

d=25,a=3.75,b=0.0039,Γ=1200.\displaystyle d=25,a=3.75,b=0.0039,\Gamma=1200. (23)

The simulations were ran long enough so as to obtain the true steady state. The relative and absolute tolerances in the difference between two values of iteration were set to 10−610^{-6} and 10−1210^{-12} respectively. We used reflective boundary conditions

∂u∂x|x=−L/2,L/2=∂v∂x|x=−L/2,L/2=0.\displaystyle\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}\Big|_{x=-L/2,L/2}=\frac{\partial v}{\partial x}\Big|_{x=-L/2,L/2}=0. (24)

except for Figure 5 and 6 Figures S5 and S7, where we use periodic boundary conditions,

u|x=−L/2=u|x=L/2,u′|x=−L/2=u′|x=L/2,v|x=−L/2=v|x=L/2,v′|x=−L/2=v′|x=L/2.\displaystyle\begin{split}u|_{x=-L/2}=u|_{x=L/2},\quad u^{\prime}|_{x=-L/2}=u^{\prime}|_{x=L/2},\\ v|_{x=-L/2}=v|_{x=L/2},\quad v^{\prime}|_{x=-L/2}=v^{\prime}|_{x=L/2}.\end{split}

The initial conditions were taken to be a random perturbation around the homogeneous steady state (drawn from a normal distribution with standard deviation of 1%).

The differential algebraic systems Eq. (10), Eq. (11) and Eq. (19) were solved using the o​d​e​15​sode15s solver.

Numerical comparisons for Figure 4

To compare the movement of peaks in the simulations with analytical calculations (spike approximation), we initialise the peaks at different positions (by translation of the steady state pattern) and monitor the evolution of the system. In Fig. 4A (single peak), we calculate the mass of the fast species, M(t)=∫−L/2L/2u(x,t)dxM(t)=\int_{-L/2}^{L/2}u(x,t)dx, and the flux on the peak Δ​Js\Delta J_{s} (Eq. (12)), at each time step as the peak approaches mid-domain. In Fig. 4C (two peaks), we generated the contours of MM by simulating the Turing system with around 200 different initial peak positions (x1,x2)(x_{1},x_{2}) (some of which are overlayed in white) and interpolating over the trajectories. Note that it is not clear how to define the flux differential across each peaks in the case of more than one peak. Similarly, in Fig. 4D, we solved the nonlinear algebraic system in Eq. (15) for different sink positions (x1,x2)(x_{1},x_{2}). We obtain at most 44 different solutions of which we take the one with the lowest total mass MM. Several analytical trajectories were obtained by solving the differential-algebraic system in Matlab consisting of Eq. (15) and Eq. (19), initialised with the solution having the lowest mass.

Appendix A Point sinks, flux balance and mass minimisation

In this appendix, we prove an important result described in the main text. The solution to Eq. (3) is given by

A⁡(x)\displaystyle A(x) =c−∑iμi′​G​(x,xi)\displaystyle=c-\sum_{i}\mu^{\prime}_{i}G(x;x_{i}) (25)

where the Green’s function is defined in Eq. (5) and the μi′=μi′​(𝒙)\mu^{\prime}_{i}=\mu^{\prime}_{i}(\bm{x}) are determined by the algebraic equations

μi′=λ⁡(c−∑jμj′​G​(xi,xj)).\mu^{\prime}_{i}=\lambda(c-\sum_{j}\mu^{\prime}_{j}G(x_{i};x_{j}))~. (26)

Properties of the Green’s function

The explicit form of the Green’s function is

G⁡(x,xi)=κ2​cosh⁡(κ​x+xiL)+cosh⁡(κ​∣x−xi∣−LL)sinh⁡(κ).\displaystyle G(x;x_{i})=\frac{\kappa}{2}\frac{\cosh{(\kappa\frac{x+x_{i}}{L})}+\cosh{(\kappa\frac{\mid x-x_{i}\mid-L}{L})}}{\sinh{(\kappa)}}~. (27)

The derivative of G⁡(x,xi)G(x;x_{i}) with respect to xx is discontinuous at x=xix=x_{i}

Gx​(x,xi)\displaystyle G_{x}(x;x_{i}) ={κ22​L​sinh⁡(κ​x+xiL)−sinh⁡(κ​xi−x−LL)sinh⁡(κ)−L2≤x<xiκ22​L​sinh⁡(κ​x+xiL)+sinh⁡(κ​x−xi−LL)sinh⁡(κ)xi<x≤L2.\displaystyle=\begin{cases}\frac{\kappa^{2}}{2L}\frac{\sinh(\kappa\frac{x+x_{i}}{L})-\sinh(\kappa\frac{x_{i}-x-L}{L})}{\sinh(\kappa)}&-\frac{L}{2}\leq x<x_{i}\\ \frac{\kappa^{2}}{2L}\frac{\sinh(\kappa\frac{x+x_{i}}{L})+\sinh(\kappa\frac{x-x_{i}-L}{L})}{\sinh(\kappa)}&x_{i}<x\leq\frac{L}{2}~.\end{cases}

Note the following property

Gx​(xi+,xj)−Gx​(xi−,xj)=−κ2L​δi​j.\displaystyle G_{x}(x_{i}^{+};x_{j})-G_{x}(x_{i}^{-};x_{j})=-\frac{\kappa^{2}}{L}\delta_{ij}~. (28)

Using this, the flux-differential Δ​Ji\Delta J_{i} defined in the main text can be written as

Δ​Ji\displaystyle\Delta J_{i} =−D2∑jμj′[Gx(xi+;xj)+Gx(xi−;xj)]\displaystyle=-\frac{D}{2}\sum_{j}\mu^{\prime}_{j}\left[G_{x}(x_{i}^{+};x_{j})+G_{x}(x_{i}^{-};x_{j})\right]
=−D∑jμj′[Gx(xi+;xj)+κ22​Lδi​j].\displaystyle=-D\sum_{j}\mu^{\prime}_{j}\left[G_{x}(x_{i}^{+};x_{j})+\frac{\kappa^{2}}{2L}\delta_{ij}\right]~. (29)

We next give some properties of the Green’s function when the sinks are called regularly positioned, i.e. when they are evenly spaced across the domain with positions

x¯i=Ln​i−L2​(1n+1),\displaystyle\bar{x}_{i}=\frac{L}{n}i-\frac{L}{2}(\frac{1}{n}+1), (30)

where x¯i\bar{x}_{i} is the position of ii th sink and nn is the total number of sinks.

Property I

Evaluating the Green’s function at the sink positions for regularly positioned sinks defines a symmetric matrix Gi​j≔G⁡(x¯i,x¯j)G_{ij}\coloneqq G(\bar{x}_{i};\bar{x}_{j}). Consider the sum of the jj column,

∑jGi​j\displaystyle\sum_{j}G_{ij} =κ2​sinh⁡(κ)​[∑j=1ncosh⁡(κ​x¯i+x¯jL)+∑j=1icosh⁡(κ​x¯i−x¯j−LL)+∑j=i+1ncosh⁡(κ​x¯j−x¯i−LL)]\displaystyle=\frac{\kappa}{2\sinh(\kappa)}\left[\sum_{j=1}^{n}\cosh(\kappa\frac{\bar{x}_{i}+\bar{x}_{j}}{L})+\sum_{j=1}^{i}\cosh(\kappa\frac{\bar{x}_{i}-\bar{x}_{j}-L}{L})+\sum_{j=i+1}^{n}\cosh(\kappa\frac{\bar{x}_{j}-\bar{x}_{i}-L}{L})\right]
=κ2​sinh⁡(κ)​[∑j=1ncosh⁡(a⁡(i+j−1−n))+∑j=1icosh⁡(a⁡(i−j−n))+∑j=i+1ncosh⁡(a⁡(j−i−n))]\displaystyle=\frac{\kappa}{2\sinh(\kappa)}\left[\sum_{j=1}^{n}\cosh(a(i+j-1-n))+\sum_{j=1}^{i}\cosh(a(i-j-n))+\sum_{j=i+1}^{n}\cosh(a(j-i-n))\right]
=κ2coth(κ2​n)∀i,\displaystyle=\frac{\kappa}{2}\coth(\frac{\kappa}{2n})\quad\forall~i, (31)

where a=κna=\frac{\kappa}{n} and the last step follows from the identity,

∑j=1ncosh⁡(a⁡(j+m))=csch⁡(a2)​sinh⁡(a​n2)​cosh⁡(a2​(2​m+n+1)).\displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{n}\cosh(a(j+m))=\csch(\frac{a}{2})\sinh(\frac{an}{2})\cosh(\frac{a}{2}(2m+n+1)).

We can similarly define a matrix Gx+G^{+}_{x} by evaluating the derivative of the Green’s function at regular positioning (Gx+)i​j=Gx​(x¯i+,x¯j)(G_{x}^{+})_{ij}=G_{x}(\bar{x}^{+}_{i};\bar{x}_{j}). Summing over the jj th column we find

∑j(Gx+)i​j\displaystyle\sum_{j}(G^{+}_{x})_{ij} =−κ22​L\displaystyle=-\frac{\kappa^{2}}{2L} (32)

by using the identity,

∑j=1nsinh⁡(a⁡(j+m))=csch⁡(a2)​sinh⁡(a​n2)​sinh⁡(a2​(2​m+n+1)).\displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{n}\sinh(a(j+m))=\csch(\frac{a}{2})\sinh(\frac{an}{2})\sinh(\frac{a}{2}(2m+n+1)).

Property II

Since the summation of GG over any of its rows or columns is the same, the vector of 11s, 𝒆^\bm{\hat{e}}, is an eigenvector of GG. Evaluating the defining equations for the 𝝁′\bm{\mu^{\prime}}, equation Eq. (26), at regular positioning 𝒙=𝒙¯\bm{x}=\bar{\bm{x}}, we obtain the matrix equation

(λ​G+1)​𝝁′​(𝒙¯)=λ​c​𝒆^.(\lambda G+1)\bm{\mu^{\prime}}(\bm{\bar{x}})=\lambda c\bm{\hat{e}}~. (33)

Since 𝒆^\bm{\hat{e}} is an eigenvector of λ​G+1\lambda G+1, we must have that

𝝁′​(𝒙¯)=C1​𝒆^,\displaystyle\bm{\mu^{\prime}}(\bm{\bar{x}})=C_{1}\bm{\hat{e}}~,

i.e. all the μi′\mu^{\prime}_{i} are identical at regular positioning or in other words, the profile of AA is symmetric. We can sum over any row and use Eq. (31) to find

μi′​(𝒙¯)=λ​c1+λ​κ2​coth⁡(κ2​n).\mu^{\prime}_{i}(\bm{\bar{x}})=\frac{\lambda c}{1+\lambda\frac{\kappa}{2}\coth{(\frac{\kappa}{2n})}}~. (34)

Regular positioning and flux balance

The flux differential across each sink is given by,

Δ​Ji\displaystyle\Delta J_{i} =−D∑jμj′[Gx(xi+;xj)+κ22​Lδi​j].\displaystyle=-D\sum_{j}\mu^{\prime}_{j}\left[G_{x}(x_{i}^{+};x_{j})+\frac{\kappa^{2}}{2L}\delta_{ij}\right]~. (35)

We evaluate this expression for regularly positioned sinks 𝒙=𝒙¯\bm{x}=\bar{\bm{x}}. First we know from equation Eq. (34) that all μj′\mu_{j}^{\prime} are identical for regularly positioned sinks. Then from equation Eq. (32), it follows that immediately that the flux-differentials vanish at regular positioning

Δ​Ji​(𝒙¯)=0∀i.\displaystyle\Delta J_{i}(\bar{\bm{x}})=0\quad\forall~i~. (36)

To show that the regularly positioned configuration is the unique configuration for which the flux-differentials vanish, we perform a power series expansion of Δ​Ji\Delta J_{i} in κ\kappa. It then suffices to show uniqueness for the κ0\kappa^{0} term. We first expand μi′\mu^{\prime}_{i} and G′​(xi,xj)G^{\prime}(x_{i};x_{j})

μi′\displaystyle\mu^{\prime}_{i} =μ0​i+μ2​i​κ2+…\displaystyle=\mu_{0i}+\mu_{2i}\kappa^{2}+...
G⁡(xi,xj)\displaystyle G(x_{i};x_{j}) =G0​(xi,xj)+G2​(xi,xj)​κ2+…\displaystyle=G_{0}(x_{i};x_{j})+G_{2}(x_{i};x_{j})\kappa^{2}+...

For the lowest order terms, we find first that G0​(xi,xj)=1G_{0}(x_{i};x_{j})=1. Inserting this into the defining equation for the μi′\mu^{\prime}_{i} (Eq. (26)), we have

μ0​i′=(c−∑jμ0​j′)​λ∀i\mu^{\prime}_{0i}=(c-\sum_{j}\mu^{\prime}_{0j})\lambda\quad\forall~i

which has solution,

μ0​i′=μ0′=λ​c1+n​λ.\mu^{\prime}_{0i}=\mu^{\prime}_{0}=\frac{\lambda c}{1+n\lambda}. (37)

We then have

Δ​Jiδ​L\displaystyle\frac{\Delta J_{i}}{\delta L} =−Dδ​L∑jμj′[Gx(xi+;xj)+κ22​Lδi​j]\displaystyle=-\frac{D}{\delta L}\sum_{j}\mu^{\prime}_{j}\left[G_{x}(x_{i}^{+};x_{j})+\frac{\kappa^{2}}{2L}\delta_{ij}\right]
=−12​[∑j=1nμj′​sinh⁡(κ​xi+xjL)sinh⁡(κ)+∑j=1iμj′​sinh⁡(κ​xi−xj−LL)sinh⁡(κ)−∑j=i+1nμj′​sinh⁡(κ​xj−xi−LL)sinh⁡(κ)+μi′]\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{2}\left[\sum_{j=1}^{n}\mu^{\prime}_{j}\frac{\sinh(\kappa\frac{x_{i}+x_{j}}{L})}{\sinh(\kappa)}+\sum_{j=1}^{i}\mu^{\prime}_{j}\frac{\sinh(\kappa\frac{x_{i}-x_{j}-L}{L})}{\sinh(\kappa)}-\sum_{j=i+1}^{n}\mu^{\prime}_{j}\frac{\sinh(\kappa\frac{x_{j}-x_{i}-L}{L})}{\sinh(\kappa)}+\mu^{\prime}_{i}\right]
=−μ0′2​L​[∑j=1n(xi+xj)+∑j=1i−1(xi−xj−L)−∑j=i+1n(xj−xi−L)]+O⁡(κ2)\displaystyle=-\frac{\mu_{0}^{\prime}}{2L}\left[\sum_{j=1}^{n}(x_{i}+x_{j})+\sum_{j=1}^{i-1}(x_{i}-x_{j}-L)-\sum_{j=i+1}^{n}(x_{j}-x_{i}-L)\right]+O(\kappa^{2})
=−n​μ0′L​[xi−Ln​i+L2​(1n+1)]+O⁡(κ2).\displaystyle=-\frac{n\mu_{0}^{\prime}}{L}\left[x_{i}-\frac{L}{n}i+\frac{L}{2}(\frac{1}{n}+1)\right]+O(\kappa^{2})~. (38)

Hence, all the flux-differentials Δ​Ji\Delta J_{i} vanish uniquely for regularly positioned sinks xi=x¯i=Ln​i−L2​(1n+1)x_{i}=\bar{x}_{i}=\frac{L}{n}i-\frac{L}{2}(\frac{1}{n}+1). If we add time-dependence to the system by specifying the sink velocities as being proportional to the their flux-differential

d​xid​t=ν​Δ​Ji​(𝒙),\frac{dx_{i}}{dt}=\nu\Delta J_{i}(\bm{x})~, (39)

then regularly positioned sinks is the unique fixed point of the resultant dynamical system (specified by the differential-algebraic system defined by equations Eq. (26), Eq. (29) and Eq. (39). Given that the domain is bounded, the fixed point is stable.

Regular positioning and mass minimisation

The total mass (or rather concentration) of AA is readily given by integrating equation Eq. (25)

M⁡(𝒙)=1L​∫−L2L2A⁡(x)​𝑑x=c−∑i=1nμi′.M(\bm{x})=\frac{1}{L}\int_{-\frac{L}{2}}^{\frac{L}{2}}A(x)dx=c-\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mu^{\prime}_{i}~. (40)

We would like to show that the regularly positioned configuration is the unique stationary point of MM. First, we will show that

∂∂xmM|𝒙=𝒙¯=−∂∂xm∑iμ′i|𝒙=𝒙¯=0.\displaystyle\left.\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{m}}M\right|_{\bm{x}=\bm{\bar{x}}}=-\left.\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{m}}\sum_{i}\mu^{\prime}_{i}\right|_{\bm{x}=\bm{\bar{x}}}=0~.

Using Eq. (26) (μi′=λ⁡(c−∑jμj′​G​(xi,xj))\mu^{\prime}_{i}=\lambda(c-\sum_{j}\mu^{\prime}_{j}G(x_{i};x_{j}))), we can evaluate the derivative of ∑iμi′\sum_{i}\mu_{i}^{\prime} with respect to an arbitrary sink position xmx_{m},

∂∂xm​∑iμi′\displaystyle\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{m}}\sum_{i}\mu^{\prime}_{i} =−λ∑i,jμj′Gxm(xi;xj)−λ∑i,jG(xi;xj)∂∂xmμj′,\displaystyle=-\lambda\sum_{i,j}\mu^{\prime}_{j}G_{x_{m}}(x_{i};x_{j})-\lambda\sum_{i,j}G(x_{i};x_{j})\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{m}}\mu^{\prime}_{j},

Evaluating this expression at regular positioning, and defining C:=∑jG⁡(x¯i,x¯j)=κ2​coth⁡(κ2​n)C:=\sum_{j}G(\bar{x}_{i};\bar{x}_{j})=\frac{\kappa}{2}\coth(\frac{\kappa}{2n}) from equation Eq. (31), we obtain

(1λ+C)​∂∂xm​∑iμi′|𝒙=𝒙¯\displaystyle\left.(\frac{1}{\lambda}+C)\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{m}}\sum_{i}\mu^{\prime}_{i}\right|_{\bm{x}=\bm{\bar{x}}} =−∑i,jμj′Gxm(xi;xj)|𝒙=𝒙¯.\displaystyle=-\left.\sum_{i,j}\mu^{\prime}_{j}G_{x_{m}}(x_{i};x_{j})\right|_{\bm{x}=\bm{\bar{x}}}.

We have already seen in equation Eq. (34) that all the μj′\mu^{\prime}_{j} are identical at regular positioning. Hence, we need only evaluate ∑i,jGxm​(xi,xj)|𝒙=𝒙¯\left.\sum_{i,j}G_{x_{m}}(x_{i};x_{j})\right|_{\bm{x}=\bm{\bar{x}}}. Inserting the definition of G⁡(xi,xj)G(x_{i};x_{j}) from equation Eq. (27) we have

∑i,jGxm​(xi,xj)|𝒙=𝒙¯=\displaystyle\left.\sum_{i,j}G_{x_{m}}(x_{i};x_{j})\right|_{\bm{x}=\bm{\bar{x}}}= κ2​sinh⁡(κ)​∑i,j∂∂xm​[cosh⁡(κ​xi+xjL)+cosh⁡(κ​|xi−xj|−LL)]|𝒙=𝒙¯\displaystyle\left.\frac{\kappa}{2\sinh(\kappa)}\sum_{i,j}\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{m}}\left[\cosh(\kappa\frac{x_{i}+x_{j}}{L})+\cosh(\kappa\frac{|x_{i}-x_{j}|-L}{L})\right]\right|_{\bm{x}=\bm{\bar{x}}}
=\displaystyle= κ22​L​sinh⁡(κ)∑i,j[δm​i(sinh(κxi+xjL)+sgn(xi−xj)sinh(κ|xi−xj|−LL))\displaystyle\frac{\kappa^{2}}{2L\sinh(\kappa)}\sum_{i,j}\left[\delta_{mi}\left(\sinh(\kappa\frac{x_{i}+x_{j}}{L})+sgn(x_{i}-x_{j})\sinh(\kappa\frac{|x_{i}-x_{j}|-L}{L})\right)\right.
+δm​j(sinh(κxi+xjL)−sgn(xi−xj)sinh(κ|xi−xj|−LL))]|𝒙=𝒙¯\displaystyle\qquad\qquad\qquad\left.+\left.\delta_{mj}\left(\sinh(\kappa\frac{x_{i}+x_{j}}{L})-sgn(x_{i}-x_{j})\sinh(\kappa\frac{|x_{i}-x_{j}|-L}{L})\right)\right]\right|_{\bm{x}=\bm{\bar{x}}}
=\displaystyle= κ2L​sinh⁡(κ)​∑i[sinh⁡(κ​xm+xiL)+s​g​n​(xm−xi)​sinh⁡(κ​|xm−xi|−LL)]|𝒙=𝒙¯\displaystyle\left.\frac{\kappa^{2}}{L\sinh(\kappa)}\sum_{i}\left[\sinh(\kappa\frac{x_{m}+x_{i}}{L})+sgn(x_{m}-x_{i})\sinh(\kappa\frac{|x_{m}-x_{i}|-L}{L})\right]\right|_{\bm{x}=\bm{\bar{x}}}
=\displaystyle= κ2L​sinh⁡(κ)​[∑i=1nsinh⁡(a⁡(m+i−n−1))+∑i=1m−1sinh⁡(a⁡(m−i−n))−∑i=m+1nsinh⁡(a⁡(i−m−n))]\displaystyle\frac{\kappa^{2}}{L\sinh(\kappa)}\left[\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sinh(a(m+i-n-1))+\sum_{i=1}^{m-1}\sinh(a(m-i-n))-\sum_{i=m+1}^{n}\sinh(a(i-m-n))\right]
=\displaystyle= κ2L​sinh⁡(κ)​[−sinh⁡(κ)−sinh⁡(−κ)]=0\displaystyle\frac{\kappa^{2}}{L\sinh(\kappa)}\left[-\sinh(\kappa)-\sinh(-\kappa)\right]=0

where the last line follows from noting that the summations are the same is in equation Eq. (32) but without the i=mi=m term. We have therefore shown that regular positioning is a stationary configuration of the total mass

∂∂xm​M|𝒙=𝒙¯=0.\left.\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{m}}M\right|_{\bm{x}=\bm{\bar{x}}}=0~.

To show that regular positioning is the unique stationary point, we proceed as in the previous section and perform a power series expansion of MM,

M=M0+M2​κ2+⋯M=M_{0}+M_{2}\kappa^{2}+\cdots (41)

It then suffices to show uniqueness for the first non-trivial order in the expansion. For the Green’s function we have

G0​(xi,xj)\displaystyle G_{0}(x_{i};x_{j}) =1,G2​(xi,xj)=xi2+xj2−L​|xi−xj|2​L2+112.\displaystyle=1,\quad G_{2}(x_{i};x_{j})=\frac{x_{i}^{2}+x_{j}^{2}-L|x_{i}-x_{j}|}{2L^{2}}+\frac{1}{12}.

We already saw that μ0​i′=μ0′=λ​c1+n​λ\mu^{\prime}_{0i}=\mu^{\prime}_{0}=\frac{\lambda c}{1+n\lambda} and hence M0M_{0} is a constant. Inserting these into the equation for μ2​i′\mu^{\prime}_{2i} using Eq. (26),

μ2​i′\displaystyle\mu^{\prime}_{2i} =−λ∑j(μ2​j′+μ0​j′G2(xi;xj)),\displaystyle=-\lambda\sum_{j}(\mu^{\prime}_{2j}+\mu^{\prime}_{0j}G_{2}(x_{i};x_{j})), (42)

we obtain

M2\displaystyle M_{2} =−∑iμ′2​i\displaystyle=-\sum_{i}\mu^{\prime}_{2i}
=λ1+n​λ​μ0′​∑i∑j(xi2+xj2−L​|xi−xj|2​L2+112).\displaystyle=\frac{\lambda}{1+n\lambda}\mu^{\prime}_{0}\sum_{i}\sum_{j}\left(\frac{x_{i}^{2}+x_{j}^{2}-L|x_{i}-x_{j}|}{2L^{2}}+\frac{1}{12}\right)~. (43)

The derivative of M2M_{2} is then proportional to

∂∂xm\displaystyle\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{m}} ∑i∑j[xi2+xj2−L​|xi−xj|]\displaystyle\sum_{i}\sum_{j}\left[x_{i}^{2}+x_{j}^{2}-L|x_{i}-x_{j}|\right]
=∂∂xm​[2​n​∑ixi2−∑i∑j≤i(xi−xj)​L−∑i∑j>i(xj−xi)​L]\displaystyle=\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{m}}\left[2n\sum_{i}x_{i}^{2}-\sum_{i}\sum_{j\leq i}(x_{i}-x_{j})L-\sum_{i}\sum_{j>i}(x_{j}-x_{i})L\right]
=∂∂xm​[2​n​∑ixi2−L⁡(∑ii​xi−∑i(n−i)​xi−∑i∑j≤ixj+∑i∑j>ixj)]\displaystyle=\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{m}}\left[2n\sum_{i}x_{i}^{2}-L(\sum_{i}ix_{i}-\sum_{i}(n-i)x_{i}-\sum_{i}\sum_{j\leq i}x_{j}+\sum_{i}\sum_{j>i}x_{j})\right]
=[4​n​xm−L⁡(m−(n−m)−(n−m+1)+m−1)]\displaystyle=\left[4nx_{m}-L(m-(n-m)-(n-m+1)+m-1)\right]
=4n[xm−Lnm+L2+L2​n)]\displaystyle=4n\left[x_{m}-\frac{L}{n}m+\frac{L}{2}+\frac{L}{2n})\right] (44)

which vanishes only for the regularly positioned configuration

xm=Ln​m−L2​(1n+1).\displaystyle x_{m}=\frac{L}{n}m-\frac{L}{2}(\frac{1}{n}+1).

Hence, we have shown that regular positioned sinks is the unique configuration for which the total mass, MM, is stationary. Based on our numerical results, we assume that this configuration is generically a minimum.

Appendix B The mass acts as a potential in the limit k→0,λ→∞k\rightarrow 0,~\lambda\rightarrow\infty

Dynamics of a single point sink

We consider the regime in which the timescale of gradient formation is much faster than that of sink movement. The profile A⁡(x)A(x) can therefore be approximated by Eq. (25). The flux differential on a single sink is given by Eq. (35),

Δ​J1\displaystyle\Delta J_{1} =−D​μ1′​[Gx​(x1+,x1)+κ22​L],\displaystyle=-D\mu^{\prime}_{1}\left[G_{x}(x_{1}^{+};x_{1})+\frac{\kappa^{2}}{2L}\right],
=−D​c​λλ​G​(x1,x1)+1​[κ2​sinh⁡(2​κ​x1/L)2​L​sinh⁡(κ)],\displaystyle=-Dc\frac{\lambda}{\lambda G(x_{1};x_{1})+1}\left[\frac{\kappa^{2}\sinh(2\kappa x_{1}/L)}{2L\sinh(\kappa)}\right], (45)

where

μ1′=λ​cλ​G​(x1,x1)+1,\mu_{1}^{\prime}=\frac{\lambda c}{\lambda G(x_{1};x_{1})+1},
G⁡(x1,x1)=κ2​[cosh⁡(2​κ​x1L)sinh⁡(κ)+coth⁡(κ)].\qquad G(x_{1};x_{1})=\frac{\kappa}{2}\left[\frac{\cosh(\frac{2\kappa x_{1}}{L})}{\sinh(\kappa)}+\coth(\kappa)\right].

Now consider the derivative of the total mass Eq. (40),

∂M∂x1\displaystyle\frac{\partial M}{\partial x_{1}} =dd​x1​(c−μ1′)=−dd​x1​μ1′\displaystyle=\frac{d}{dx_{1}}(c-\mu^{\prime}_{1})=-\frac{d}{dx_{1}}\mu^{\prime}_{1}
=−c​(λλ​G​(x1,x1)+1)2​κ2​sinh⁡(2​κ​x1/L)L​sinh⁡(κ).\displaystyle=-c\left(\frac{\lambda}{\lambda G(x_{1};x_{1})+1}\right)^{2}\frac{\kappa^{2}\sinh{(2\kappa x_{1}/L)}}{L\sinh(\kappa)}~. (46)

In the limit κ→0\kappa\rightarrow 0 we can see that easily that G⁡(x1,x1)=1G(x_{1};x_{1})=1. If sinks are also much stronger than the background decay rate i.e. λ≫1\lambda\gg 1, then we obtain the following relation,

Δ​J=−D2​∂M∂x1.\Delta J=-\frac{D}{2}\frac{\partial M}{\partial x_{1}}~.

Hence, in that limit the velocity of a single point sink can be written equivalently in terms of the derivative of total mass MM as,

d​x1d​t\displaystyle\frac{dx_{1}}{dt} =ν​Δ​J1\displaystyle=\nu\Delta J_{1}
=−ν​D2​∂M∂x1.\displaystyle=-\nu\frac{D}{2}\frac{\partial M}{\partial x_{1}}~. (47)

In the next subsection, we generalise this relation to nn arbitrary sinks.

Dynamics of n sinks

We consider again the limit κ≪1\kappa\ll 1. Then, the flux differential up to lowest order in κ\kappa is given by Eq. (38),

Δ​Jic​δ​L=−nL​λ1+n​λ​[xi−Ln​i+L2​(1n+1)]+O⁡(k2),\displaystyle\begin{split}\frac{\Delta J_{i}}{c\delta L}&=-\frac{n}{L}\frac{\lambda}{1+n\lambda}\left[x_{i}-\frac{L}{n}i+\frac{L}{2}(\frac{1}{n}+1)\right]+O(k^{2}),\end{split} (48)

where we have used the expression for the lowest order term of μ′\mu^{\prime} from Eq. (37),

μ0′=λ​c1+n​λ.\mu^{\prime}_{0}=\frac{\lambda c}{1+n\lambda}.

The derivative of MM up to second order in κ\kappa from Eq. (44),

Dc​δ​L​∂M∂xi=(λ1+n​λ)2​∂∂xi​∑i,jG2​(xi,xj)+O⁡(k4),=2​nL​(λ1+n​λ)2​[xi−Ln​i+L2​(1n+1)]+O⁡(k4)\displaystyle\begin{split}\frac{D}{c\delta L}\frac{\partial M}{\partial x_{i}}&=\left(\frac{\lambda}{1+n\lambda}\right)^{2}\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{i}}\sum_{i,j}G_{2}(x_{i};x_{j})+O(k^{4}),\\ &=\frac{2n}{L}\left(\frac{\lambda}{1+n\lambda}\right)^{2}\left[x_{i}-\frac{L}{n}i+\frac{L}{2}(\frac{1}{n}+1)\right]+O(k^{4})\end{split} (49)

where we have used the second order expansion of G⁡(xi,xj)G(x_{i};x_{j}) in κ\kappa (Eq. (44)). Taken together the above equations in the limit λ≫1\lambda\gg 1 imply,

Δ​Ji=−12​n​D​∂M∂xi.\displaystyle\begin{split}\Delta J_{i}=-\frac{1}{2}nD\frac{\partial M}{\partial x_{i}}~.\end{split} (50)

Therefore in that limit the dynamics of the point sinks are equivalently specified by

d​x1d​t=−ν​n2​D​∂M∂xi.\displaystyle\frac{dx_{1}}{dt}=-\nu\frac{n}{2}D\frac{\partial M}{\partial x_{i}}~. (51)

Hence for large diffusive length scale κ≪1\kappa\ll 1 and strong sinks λ≫1\lambda\gg 1, the dynamics of the system is akin to damped particles moving in a potential specified by the total mass. It should be noted that away from this limit, while the dynamics may be different, the two prescriptions share the same stationary points. However, for our parameter choices we found very good agreement between the two systems (Fig. 3D).

Appendix C Peak Movement and Pattern selection in the Brusselator

We now present an analysis of Brusselator and show numerically and analytically that most of the features of the exploratory model in Eq. (2) still holds.

The general spatial version of Brusselator [43] is described by the following equations,

∂u∂t=Du​∂2u∂x2−β​u​v2+γ​v∂v∂t=Dv​∂2v∂x2+β​u​v2−γ​v+δ​c−δ​v.\displaystyle\begin{split}\frac{\partial u}{\partial t}&=D_{u}\frac{\partial^{2}u}{\partial x^{2}}-\beta uv^{2}+\gamma v\\ \frac{\partial v}{\partial t}&=D_{v}\frac{\partial^{2}v}{\partial x^{2}}+\beta uv^{2}-\gamma v+\delta c-\delta v~.\end{split} (52)

In the absence of diffusion it has a single fixed point. The model also has the form of a mass-conserving Turing system with additional linear terms. However, note that rather than total mass being fixed at steady state, it is the mass of vv that is fixed

1L​∫v¯​𝑑x=c.\frac{1}{L}\int\bar{v}~dx=c~. (53)

As before, by writing the source term as δ​c\delta c we can change the turnover δ\delta without affecting the steady state concentration of vv. We non-dimensionalise the system by

x→xL,t→Dv​tL2,u→uc,v→vc\displaystyle x\to\frac{x}{L},t\to\frac{D_{v}t}{L^{2}},u\to\frac{u}{c},v\to\frac{v}{c}

to obtain

∂u∂t\displaystyle\frac{\partial u}{\partial t} =d​∂2u∂x2+Γ⁡(−a​u​v2+v)\displaystyle=d\frac{\partial^{2}u}{\partial x^{2}}+\Gamma\Big(-auv^{2}+v\Big) (54a)
∂v∂t\displaystyle\frac{\partial v}{\partial t} =∂2v∂x2+Γ⁡(a​u​v2−v+b⁡(1−v))\displaystyle=\frac{\partial^{2}v}{\partial x^{2}}+\Gamma\Big(auv^{2}-v+b(1-v)\Big) (54b)

where

Γ=γ​L2Dv,d=DuDv,a=β​c2γ,b=δγ.\displaystyle\Gamma=\frac{\gamma L^{2}}{D_{v}},d=\frac{D_{u}}{D_{v}},a=\frac{\beta c^{2}}{\gamma},b=\frac{\delta}{\gamma}~.

The fixed point is,

u0=1a,v0=1.\displaystyle u_{0}=\frac{1}{a},v_{0}=1~.

The Jacobian is given by,

J(u0,v0)=Γ​[−a​v02−2​a​u0​v0+1a​v022​a​u0​v0−1−b]\displaystyle J_{(u_{0},v_{0})}=\Gamma\begin{bmatrix}-av_{0}^{2}&-2au_{0}v_{0}+1\\ av_{0}^{2}&2au_{0}v_{0}-1-b\end{bmatrix} =Γ​[−a−1a1−b].\displaystyle=\Gamma\begin{bmatrix}-a&-1\\ a&1-b\end{bmatrix}~.

The Jacobian (and hence the dispersion relation) becomes independent of bb for b<<1b<<1. Hence, we can change bb without significantly affecting the linear behaviour of the model. The trace and determinant of the Jacobian are easily found to be,

T​r​J=Γ⁡(1−a−b)D​e​t​J=Γ2​a​b.\displaystyle\begin{split}TrJ&=\Gamma(1-a-b)\\ DetJ&=\Gamma^{2}ab~.\end{split}

For the homogeneous fixed point to be stable in the absence of diffusion we also need T​r​J<0TrJ<0 and D​e​t​J>0DetJ>0. Hence, we require a+b>1a+b>1. The Turing condition for the Brusselator is given by,

d⁡(1−b)−a−2​d​a​b>0.\displaystyle d(1-b)-a-2\sqrt{dab}>0.

We numerically solve this system, using reflexive boundary condition, by perturbing the homogeneous state as described in numerical method. Like in our model, and every Turing model we are aware of, the interior peaks of a pattern are periodic and regularly positioned. Furthermore, consistent with our results, a single peak moves exponentially to mid-domain (Figure S6A). The rate of movement was found to be proportional to bb, or equivalently, δ\delta, the turnover rate and for b=0b=0 no peak movement is observed.

In Figure 6A we switch to periodic boundary conditions as in Figure 5 and compare the number of peaks in the dominant mode as predicted by the linear dispersion relation and the number of peaks in the most frequent pattern as obtained from the numerical simulations. As in the main text, we replace bb by κ=b​Γd\kappa=\sqrt{\frac{b\Gamma}{d}}, the ratio of the length of the domain to the diffusive length-scale, which we find to be a more physical parameter (the dimensionless variables are then Γ\Gamma, dd, aa and κ\kappa). We observed a similar coarsening behaviour as the turnover rate is decreased (and the diffusive length-scale lengthened) as in the exploratory model (Figure 5A,B), where the number of peaks in the final pattern is fewer than what is predicted by linear stability analysis for lower values of κ\kappa.

Mass minimization predicts the pattern obtained after coarsening

In this section, we derive an analytical expression for the mass of the fast species in the Brusselator model in the spike limit. Let us consider the dimensionless form in Eq. (54). As in the case of our toy model we consider the limit Dv≪D​uD_{v}\ll Du, where solutions of vv consist of narrow large-amplitude spikes, defined to have width ϵ\epsilon. Away from the spikes vv is a spatial constant vo​u​tv_{out}. Since ∫−1/21/2vdx=1\int_{-1/2}^{1/2}vdx=1, inside the spikes we have v≫1v\gg 1 and outside v=vo​u​t≪1v=v_{out}\ll 1. We search for steady state solutions consisting of nn spikes at xi={x1,x2,…,xn}x_{i}=\{x_{1},x_{2},...,x_{n}\} and assume that uu changes slowly within each spike and can be approximated by a constant uiu_{i}. We shift to an inner coordinate y=ϵ−1​(x−xi)y=\epsilon^{-1}(x-x_{i}), within each spike. The equation for the inner variable vi​(y)v_{i}(y) becomes,

1ϵ2​d2​vid​yi2+Γ⁡(a​ui​v2−(b+1)​v)=0,\displaystyle\frac{1}{\epsilon^{2}}\frac{d^{2}v_{i}}{dy_{i}^{2}}+\Gamma(au_{i}v^{2}-(b+1)v)=0,
vi→0​ as ​yi→±∞,\displaystyle v_{i}\to 0\text{ as }y_{i}\to\pm\infty,

where we have neglected the constant term since vi≫1v_{i}\gg 1. The solution to this equation is

vi=32​b+1a​ui​sech2​(b+12​ϵ​yi2).\displaystyle v_{i}=\frac{3}{2}\frac{b+1}{au_{i}}\text{sech}^{2}(\frac{\sqrt{b+1}}{2}\frac{\epsilon y_{i}}{2}).

In the outer region the equation each spike is approximated by a Dirac delta function

v=vo​u​t+∑iwi1​δ​(x−xi),v=v_{out}+\sum_{i}w_{i_{1}}\delta(x-x_{i})~, (55)

where wi1w_{i_{1}} is the weight

wi1=ϵ​∫−∞∞vi​(yi)​d​yi=6a​ui​b+1Γ.w_{i_{1}}=\epsilon\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}v_{i}(y_{i})dy_{i}=\frac{6}{au_{i}}\sqrt{\frac{b+1}{\Gamma}}~.

The ϵ\epsilon pre-factor is the spike width. To write the outer equation for uu, we also need the weight of the u​v2uv^{2} term

wi2=ϵ​a​ui​∫−∞∞vi2​(yi)​d​yi=6a​ui​(b+1)3/2Γ.w_{i_{2}}=\epsilon au_{i}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}v^{2}_{i}(y_{i})dy_{i}=\frac{6}{au_{i}}\frac{(b+1)^{3/2}}{\sqrt{\Gamma}}~. (56)

The spike contribution from the −u​v2+v-uv^{2}+v is then

−wi​1+wi​2=6​ba​ui​b+1Γ.\displaystyle-w_{i1}+w_{i2}=\frac{6b}{au_{i}}\sqrt{\frac{b+1}{\Gamma}}~. (57)

Finally since vo​u​t≪1v_{out}\ll 1, we neglect the u​vo​u​t2uv^{2}_{out} term. The outer equation for uu becomes,

d​d2​ud​x2−Γ⁡(∑i=1n6​ba​ui​(b+1)Γ​δ​(x−xi))+Γ​vo​u​t=0,\displaystyle d\frac{d^{2}u}{dx^{2}}-\Gamma\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{6b}{au_{i}}\sqrt{\frac{(b+1)}{\Gamma}}\delta(x-x_{i})\right)+\Gamma v_{out}=0~,
−1/2<x<1/2,ux(±1/2)=0.\displaystyle\qquad-1/2<x<1/2,~~u_{x}(\pm 1/2)=0~. (58)

Integrating the above equation over the whole domain we obtain,

∑i1ui\displaystyle\sum_{i}\frac{1}{u_{i}} =a​vo​u​t6​b​Γb+1.\displaystyle=\frac{av_{out}}{6b}\sqrt{\frac{\Gamma}{b+1}}~. (59)

In the outer region, vv appears almost flat, hence we can approximate Eq. (54b) as,

a​u​vo​u​t2−(b+1)​vo​u​t+b=0.auv_{out}^{2}-(b+1)v_{out}+b=0~.

This implies vo​u​t=bb+1v_{out}=\frac{b}{b+1}, where we ignore the cubic term as vo​u​t≪1v_{out}\ll 1. The expression is alternatively obtained by using Eq. (55) the integral condition ∫v​𝑑x=1\int vdx=1. The solution to the outer equation now is,

u⁡(x)=u¯+6​ba​(b+1)Γ​∑j=1n1uj​G​(x,xj),\displaystyle u(x)=\bar{u}+\frac{6b}{a}\sqrt{\frac{(b+1)}{\Gamma}}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\frac{1}{u_{j}}G(x;x_{j}), (60)

where u¯\bar{u} is a constant and the Green’s function G⁡(x,xj)G(x;x_{j}) is the solution to

D2​Gx​x​(x,xj)+1\displaystyle\frac{D}{2}G_{xx}(x;x_{j})+1 =δ(x−xj),−1/2<x<1/2,\displaystyle=\delta(x-x_{j}),\quad-1/2<x<1/2,
Gx(±1/2)\displaystyle\quad G_{x}(\pm 1/2) =0,∫−1/21/2G(x;xj)dx=0\displaystyle=0,\quad\int_{-1/2}^{1/2}G(x;x_{j})dx=0

given by

G⁡(x,xj)=−1D​(x2+xj2)+1D​∣x−xj∣−16​D.\displaystyle G(x;x_{j})=-\frac{1}{D}(x^{2}+x_{j}^{2})+\frac{1}{D}\mid x-x_{j}\mid-\frac{1}{6D}.

We identify the coefficient DD in the above equations as, D=2​dΓD=\frac{2d}{\Gamma}. The constant u¯\bar{u} in Eq. (60) is determined by the condition for uiu_{i},

u⁡(xi)=ui=u¯+6​ba​(b+1)Γ​∑j=1n1uj​G​(xi,xj).\displaystyle u(x_{i})=u_{i}=\bar{u}+\frac{6b}{a}\sqrt{\frac{(b+1)}{\Gamma}}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\frac{1}{u_{j}}G(x_{i};x_{j}).

Now we consider the situation where the spikes are symmetric (ui=ucu_{i}=u_{c}) and regularly positioned,

x¯i=Ln​i−L2​(1n+1)\displaystyle\bar{x}_{i}=\frac{L}{n}i-\frac{L}{2}(\frac{1}{n}+1)

as in the analysis in the main text. For convenience, we also use reflexive rather than periodic conditions as the solutions only differ by an arbitrary phase. From Eq. (59), we then have

uc=6a​(b+1)3/2Γ​n.\displaystyle u_{c}=\frac{6}{a}\frac{(b+1)^{3/2}}{\sqrt{\Gamma}}n.

The equation for u⁡(xi)u(x_{i}) becomes,

u⁡(xi¯)=uc=u¯+6​ba​(b+1)Γ​1uc​∑j=1nG⁡(xi¯,xj¯).\displaystyle u(\bar{x_{i}})=u_{c}=\bar{u}+\frac{6b}{a}\sqrt{\frac{(b+1)}{\Gamma}}\frac{1}{u_{c}}\sum_{j=1}^{n}G(\bar{x_{i}};\bar{x_{j}}).

Evaluating the sum in the above equation we find an expression independent of ii,

∑j=1nG⁡(xi¯,xj¯)=−16​D​n\displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{n}G(\bar{x_{i}};\bar{x_{j}})=-\frac{1}{6Dn}

and determine that the constant u¯\bar{u} which is in fact the total mass MM of the fast species

M=∫−1/21/2u(x)dx\displaystyle M=\int_{-1/2}^{1/2}u(x)dx =∫−1/21/2u¯dx=6​n​(b+1)3/2a​Γ+1n2Γ​b12​d​(b+1),\displaystyle=\int_{-1/2}^{1/2}\bar{u}~dx=\frac{6n(b+1)^{3/2}}{a\sqrt{\Gamma}}+\frac{1}{n^{2}}\frac{\Gamma b}{12d(b+1)}, (61)

where we have used the Green’s function property ∫−1/21/2G(x;xj)=0\int_{-1/2}^{1/2}G(x;x_{j})=0. Note MM is minimal for a critical number of peaks n=ncn=n_{c}.

In Figure 6C, we compare the number of peaks of the final pattern obtained after coarsening (black line in Figure 6A) with ncn_{c} and the linear prediction. We find that, like in the model of the main text, ncn_{c} is an excellent predictor of number of peaks in the steady state pattern.
